title: Setting Up Go: go run, build, install
summary: The three commands you'll reach for constantly are `go run` (compile and execute in one shot), `go build` (compile to a binary you can ship), and `go install` (compile and place a binary on your PATH). Knowing exactly what each does — and where its output goes — is the foundation of a smooth Go workflow.

subtopics.title: go run: compile + run, no leftover binary
subtopics.explanation: `go run` compiles your program to a temporary file, runs it, then discards the binary. It's perfect for quick iteration and scripts because you never see a build artifact — but it recompiles every time, so it's not for production.
subtopics.example:
go run .          # run the package in the current dir
go run main.go    # run a single file

subtopics.title: go build: produce a shippable binary
subtopics.explanation: `go build` compiles your package into an executable in the current directory (named after the module/dir) without running it. This is the artifact you copy to a server or into a container.
subtopics.example:
go build -o server .  # writes ./server
./server              # run it

subtopics.title: go install: put the binary on your PATH
subtopics.explanation: `go install` compiles and copies the resulting binary into your GOBIN directory (default $HOME/go/bin), so if that's on your PATH you can run the tool by name from anywhere. It's how you install CLI tools.

subtopics.title: Where things go: GOBIN, GOPATH, PATH
subtopics.explanation: `go install` writes to GOBIN if set, otherwise to $GOPATH/bin (default $HOME/go/bin). To run installed tools by name, that directory must be on your shell PATH. `go env` shows all these settings.
subtopics.example:
go env GOBIN GOPATH
export PATH=$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin

subtopics.title: Cross-compilation with GOOS/GOARCH
subtopics.explanation: Go can build for other operating systems and CPUs without extra toolchains by setting GOOS (target OS) and GOARCH (target CPU). This is how you build a Linux server binary from a Mac laptop.

foundations.overview: Once you can write a Go program, you need to turn it into something that runs. Go gives you three closely-related commands. `go run` is for fast feedback while developing: it compiles and immediately executes, leaving nothing behind. `go build` is for producing a binary you can keep, deploy, or put in a container. `go install` is for installing command-line tools: it builds and drops the binary into a known directory on your PATH so you can invoke it by name. Understanding the difference — especially where each one puts its output — removes a huge amount of beginner confusion.
foundations.formalDefinition: go run compiles and executes the named package without retaining the executable; go build compiles packages into an executable (or checks library packages) in the working directory; go install compiles and installs the resulting binary into the Go bin directory (GOBIN or $GOPATH/bin).
foundations.whyItMatters: These commands are the bridge between your source code and a running program. Every development loop, CI build, and deployment step uses one of them, so misunderstanding where the binary lands is a daily friction point for beginners.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a kitchen: `go run` cooks and serves the dish immediately, washing the pan after (no leftovers). `go build` plates a dish to take home (a binary in your hands). `go install` puts the dish in the shared fridge (your PATH) so anyone can grab it later by name.
foundations.runtimePerspective: All three invoke the same compiler and linker. The only differences are what happens to the output: run executes a temp file and deletes it, build writes to the current directory, install writes to the bin directory. The compiler caches results, so repeated builds of unchanged code are fast.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Developers use `go run .` while iterating, CI uses `go build` to produce deployable artifacts, and `go install tool@version` is the standard way to add Go-based CLI tools like golangci-lint or stringer.
foundations.businessImpact: Fast, cached compiles keep developer feedback loops tight, and reproducible build commands make CI/CD pipelines simple and reliable, reducing time-to-ship.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing the output locations prevents 'command not found' confusion and accidental commits of binaries; cross-compilation lets one machine build artifacts for every target.
foundations.performanceImpact: go build caches compiled packages, so incremental builds are quick; go run recompiles each invocation, which is fine for development but wasteful for repeated production runs.
commonUseCases: go run . for rapid local iteration
go build -o app . to produce a deployable binary
go install tool@version to add CLI tools to PATH

commonMisconceptions.myth: go run creates a binary in my folder.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It compiles to a temporary location and removes the executable after running; nothing is left in your directory.
It compiles and copies the binary to the bin directory; you then run it by name. It does not execute your program for you.
Pure-Go code cross-compiles with just GOOS/GOARCH set; you only need a C toolchain when using cgo.

visualExplorer.title: run vs build vs install
visualExplorer.caption: Same compiler, three different destinations for the output.

config.intro: What each command does with the compiled output:

steps.name: go run
steps.detail: Compiles to a temporary file, executes it immediately, then deletes it. Best for quick iteration; leaves no artifact.

steps.name: go build
steps.detail: Compiles to an executable in the current directory (use -o to name it). Does NOT run it. This is your deployable artifact.

steps.name: go install
steps.detail: Compiles, then copies the binary into GOBIN (or $GOPATH/bin). If that dir is on PATH, you run the tool by name.

steps.name: Cross-target
steps.detail: Set GOOS/GOARCH before build/install to produce binaries for other OS/CPU combinations from the same machine.

interactiveExamples.title: Run, then build the same program
interactiveExamples.explanation: This program prints a line. With `go run main.go` you see the output and no file appears. With `go build -o hello main.go` you get a ./hello binary you can run repeatedly.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: report the build target
interactiveExamples.explanation: The runtime package exposes the OS and architecture the binary was built for. Fill in the call to print them, then imagine cross-compiling with GOOS=linux to see the value change.

checkpoints.prompt: You run `go run main.go`. Where is the executable afterward?
options: Nowhere — it was compiled to a temp file and deleted
checkpoints.explanation: go run compiles to a temporary location, executes, and removes the binary. To keep an artifact use go build; to place it on PATH use go install.

checkpoints.prompt: Compile the current package into a binary named 'server' without running it.
checkpoints.explanation: go build -o server . compiles the current package and names the output 'server'. go run would execute and discard it; go install would place it in the bin dir; go fmt formats code.

checkpoints.prompt: After `go install`, you type the tool's name and get 'command not found'. Most likely cause?
options: The tool failed to compile silently
Your GOBIN/$GOPATH/bin directory isn't on your PATH
checkpoints.explanation: go install puts the binary in GOBIN (or $HOME/go/bin). If that directory isn't on your PATH, the shell can't find it. Add it: export PATH=$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin.

checkpoints.prompt: What command builds a Linux amd64 binary from a Mac?
checkpoints.explanation: Cross-compilation in Go is driven by the GOOS (target OS) and GOARCH (target CPU) environment variables set before go build. Pure-Go code needs no extra toolchain.

codeLab.title: Report the runtime environment
codeLab.instructions: Implement `BuildTarget() string` that returns the build target in the form "<os>/<arch>" using the runtime package (e.g. "linux/amd64"). This is the kind of info you'd log at startup.
hints: runtime.GOOS gives the OS string; runtime.GOARCH gives the CPU architecture.
Concatenate with a literal "/" between them.

debuggingLab.title: I built it but nothing happened
debuggingLab.symptom: You run `go build .` expecting output, but the terminal just returns to the prompt with no printed message.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: go build only compiles — it does not run your program. It produced a binary in the current directory; you still have to execute it. The lack of output is expected behavior, not an error.
commonMistakes: Expecting go build to run the program like go run does.
Not realizing a binary was created and needs to be invoked (./<name>).
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Either use go run to compile-and-execute, or run the produced binary.

solution.code:
// Option A: compile and run in one step
$ go run .
hi

// Option B: build then execute the artifact
$ go build -o app .
$ ./app
hi

theory.question: Explain the difference between go run, go build, and go install.
theory.directAnswer: go run compiles to a temporary executable, runs it, and discards it — great for iteration. go build compiles to an executable in the current directory but does not run it — that's your deployable artifact. go install compiles and copies the binary into the Go bin directory (GOBIN or $GOPATH/bin) so you can run it by name if that's on your PATH.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Three subcommands that compile with the same toolchain but place output differently.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Different stages of the workflow need different outcomes: quick run, shippable artifact, or installed tool.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: run -> temp + execute + delete; build -> ./binary; install -> bin dir on PATH.

theory.whyImportant: Confusing them causes the classic 'where did my binary go / why didn't it run' beginner mistakes.
theory.realWorldExample: CI runs go build to produce the artifact; developers use go run locally; go install adds linters and code generators.

followUps.question: Does go build run tests?
followUps.answer: No — tests run with go test. go build only compiles.

followUps.question: How do you name the build output?
followUps.answer: Use the -o flag, e.g. go build -o server .

theory.question: How does cross-compilation work in Go, and what do you need?
theory.directAnswer: Set the GOOS (target operating system) and GOARCH (target CPU architecture) environment variables before go build. For pure-Go programs that's all you need — no separate cross-toolchain. You only need a C cross-compiler when your code uses cgo.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Building a binary for a different OS/CPU than the machine you're on.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Teams develop on Macs/Windows but deploy to Linux servers and containers.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The Go toolchain ships compilers for many targets; GOOS/GOARCH select which one to use.

theory.whyImportant: Almost every container build cross-compiles to linux/amd64 or linux/arm64.
theory.realWorldExample: GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -o server . produces a Linux binary on a developer's Mac for a Docker image.

followUps.question: How do you produce a fully static binary?
followUps.answer: Set CGO_ENABLED=0 so the binary doesn't link against libc, ideal for FROM scratch images.

scenario.question: A teammate installed a Go CLI with `go install tool@latest` but can't run it by name. How do you diagnose and fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: The binary was placed in the Go bin directory but that directory isn't on their PATH. Check with `go env GOPATH` and `go env GOBIN`; the binary is in GOBIN or $GOPATH/bin (default ~/go/bin). Add that directory to PATH (export PATH=$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin) and reload the shell.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A PATH configuration gap, not a build failure.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: go install only copies the binary to the bin dir; making it runnable by name is the shell's job.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The shell searches PATH directories for the command name; if the bin dir isn't listed, lookup fails.

scenario.whyImportant: This is the single most common stumbling block when installing Go tools.
scenario.realWorldExample: Adding $(go env GOPATH)/bin to PATH in .zshrc fixes golangci-lint, stringer, and similar tools.

followUps.question: Where does go install put the binary if GOBIN is set?
followUps.answer: Directly into GOBIN, overriding the default $GOPATH/bin.

coding.question: Write a small program that prints its own build target and the Go version it was compiled with.
coding.thoughtProcess: The runtime package exposes GOOS, GOARCH, and Version(). Print them in a readable line. This is a common startup-log pattern.
coding.lineByLine: runtime.GOOS and runtime.GOARCH are constants fixed at compile time describing the target. runtime.Version() returns the Go toolchain version string. Printf formats them into one line ending in a newline.

followUps.question: Would GOOS change if you cross-compile?
followUps.answer: Yes — building with GOOS=linux makes runtime.GOOS report "linux" in that binary.

followUps.question: How could you embed a git commit at build time?
followUps.answer: Use -ldflags "-X main.version=..." to set a package-level variable during go build.

productionDeepDive.architecture: CI/CD pipelines standardize on go build (often cross-compiled to linux) to produce a single artifact, then bake it into a minimal container image. Reproducible build commands keep environments consistent.
productionDeepDive.performance: Go's build cache makes incremental builds fast; avoid go run in production loops since it recompiles each time. Use prebuilt binaries for deployment.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Build commands themselves parallelize package compilation across cores, so large modules build quickly.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Pin tool versions with go install tool@v1.2.3 (not @latest) in CI for reproducible builds; build with CGO_ENABLED=0 to avoid host-libc surprises.
productionDeepDive.observability: Embed version/commit info via -ldflags -X so running binaries can report exactly what was built, aiding incident triage.
productionDeepDive.security: Static binaries (CGO_ENABLED=0) in scratch/distroless images minimize the attack surface; fewer OS packages mean fewer CVEs to patch.

caseStudies.problem: Need identical, reproducible artifacts across many machines.
caseStudies.solution: Standardize GOOS/GOARCH and pin tool versions in go install commands.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly more setup vs. far fewer 'works on my machine' issues.
caseStudies.lessons: Make build commands explicit and reproducible; never rely on @latest in CI.

caseStudies.solution: Cross-compile a static binary with CGO_ENABLED=0 into FROM scratch.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: No shell in the image for debugging.
caseStudies.lessons: Single static binaries make tiny, secure images possible.

keyTakeaways: go run compiles and executes immediately, leaving no binary — use it for fast iteration.
go build compiles to a binary in the current directory (name it with -o) but does not run it — that's your deployable artifact.
go install puts the binary in GOBIN/$GOPATH/bin; add that directory to PATH to run installed tools by name.
Cross-compile pure-Go code with GOOS/GOARCH, and CGO_ENABLED=0 for fully static binaries.
